1. Core Clinical Tension: A patient presenting with bilateral acute-on-chronic subdural hematomas after a minor head trauma one month prior creates an overwhelming presumption of simple traumatic intracranial hemorrhage; the underlying driver—a life-threatening microvascular coagulopathy secondary to Plasmodium infection causing rapid multi-compartment recurrent intracranial bleeds—remains covert because baseline platelet counts and routine coagulation profiles are initially normal.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The admission triage evaluation ends when emergency non-contrast cranial CT identifies bilateral acute-on-chronic subdural hematomas with midline shift requiring emergent neurosurgical intervention, immediately prior to postoperative re-bleeding episodes and specialized hematologic/parasitologic testing.
3. Differential Distinctions: Uncomplicated traumatic subdural hematoma ceases bleeding following surgical evacuation; dengue hemorrhagic fever or inherited factor deficiencies (e.g., Factor XIII deficiency) produce distinct serological/antigenic positivity or factor assay reductions; Plasmodium-induced coagulopathy triggers catastrophic recurrent intracranial bleeding that halts specifically upon intravenous artesunate administration.
case_prompt: A previously healthy 53-year-old male was brought to the emergency department by his family due to severe, continuous headache accompanied by vomiting for 5 days. He also experienced dizziness, progressive difficulty walking, and increasing drowsiness over the preceding 24 hours. History revealed that he had been involved in a road traffic accident one month prior, which resulted in a mild cerebral contusion and a small right frontal hematoma that had been managed conservatively without surgical intervention. He had no other known chronic medical conditions and took no regular medications. On initial triage evaluation, his Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score was 13/15, and his pupils were equal, round, and reactive to light bilaterally. Routine triage laboratory testing revealed a hemoglobin level of 10.9 g/dL and a platelet count of 169 x 10^3/mL. Because his consciousness subsequently began to deteriorate rapidly, an emergent non-contrast computed tomography (CT) scan of the head was performed, which demonstrated bilateral acute-on-chronic subdural hematomas with significant midline shift and subfalcine herniation toward the right hemisphere, prompting immediate emergency neurosurgical evaluation.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: A road traffic accident one month earlier and acute-on-chronic subdural hematomas initially pointed to traumatic hemorrhage; however, fulminant consecutive postoperative re-bleeding in multiple compartments (subdural, extradural, and frontal intraparenchymal) despite prompt evacuations signaled an underlying acquired bleeding diathesis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Upon inquiry, it was disclosed that the patient had been involved in a road traffic accident (RTA) 1 month prior, resulting in a mild contusion and right frontal lobe hematoma, which was managed conservatively [Figure 1a and b].

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: In an endemic setting, acute headache, vomiting, and severe intracranial hemorrhagic diathesis strongly prompted testing for dengue virus; however, dengue diagnostic testing returned negative.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Platelet aggregation studies, fibrinogen, factor 13, and other clotting tests were conducted, alongside tests for malaria and dengue, which returned positive for Falciparum species. The remaining conventional clotting tests were normal, and dengue was negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Congenital or Consumptive Coagulopathy (e.g., Factor XIII deficiency)
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Repeated surgical re-bleeding with normal standard screening coagulation assays raised concern for hidden factor deficiencies such as Factor XIII or platelet aggregation disorders; however, specialized factor assays and aggregation panels were normal.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The remaining conventional clotting tests were normal, and dengue was negative.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Blood testing returned positive for Plasmodium falciparum, identifying falciparum malaria-induced microvascular sequestration and coagulopathy as the cause of recurrent intracranial hemorrhage, leading to rapid clinical stabilization upon initiation of intravenous artesunate.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Due to the consecutive recurrent intracranial bleeds, a hematology consultation was sought. Platelet aggregation studies, fibrinogen, factor 13, and other clotting tests were conducted, alongside tests for malaria and dengue, which returned positive for Falciparum species.

editor_comments: Standardized admission diagnostic case. Case prompt halts at emergency CT revealing acute-on-chronic SDH and baseline labs. Operative course, re-bleeding, and parasitic identification strictly excluded from prompt. Verbatim quotes provided.
